utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to say good morning to all those present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. I'm going to start off by giving the floor to the registrar for the IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The OTP submitted a response to 3D objections regarding OTP exhibits tendered through Witness CT. That shall be given Exhibit number IC 220. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness CU. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 221. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 222. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 223. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 224. The list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 225, and the list submitted by 6D shall be given Exhibit number IC 226. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'm going to read an important oral decision now. I'm going to read it slowly so that everybody can take note of it. Oral decision relating to the procedure to follow with respect to the requests for protective measures for witnesses. In order to ensure efficacious work, the Trial Chamber wishes to regulate procedure with respect to the protection of witnesses in future in the following manner: When the Prosecution wishes to make a submission for protective measures for its witnesses, it will have to, in written form, file a submission for protective measures, for allowing protective measures to be put in place. This request must be made simultaneously with the schedule for each particular month or, at the latest, this must be submitted one week before the appearance of the first witness on our schedule. This request on the part of the Prosecution must incorporate and set out all the protective measures that they are requesting for that particular witness, and it relates to the witness that has been provided for in the schedule for the upcoming court proceedings. The Defence will have one week at its disposal after the Prosecution files its request to respond if they wish to object. These objections, or any objections that the Defence wishes to make, must be set out in written form, in a written response. I'm now going to recapitulate the procedure, summarise it. From now on, when the Prosecution prepares its schedule and timetable for our work, which includes the names of witnesses for a given month, if the Prosecution wishes to ask for protective measures for any of those witnesses on the schedule, then they must file a written submission, a written request, stating the reasons for which they are asking protective measures. Once this submission is filed, the Defence will have one week to decide whether it wishes to object or not, and if they do, this should be done in writing. That means that we're not going to have any more debate in the courtroom as we had to do last time when we spent one hour discussing protective measures. So this way everything will be regulated in writing. I'm now going to ask Mr. Registrar for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you can tell the witness, as we're in open session, that he refrain from naming any names, and if he wishes to do so, we can go into private session to hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard the Judge, and I think you know what the situation is like. You're now in open session, and your face will be distorted. So don't mention your name now, but as protective measures have been granted, your image will not go out of the courtroom. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I'll be referring to you as Witness CV. That will be your pseudonym. Witness, is it correct that you were born and raised in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was your profession before the war against the Serbs -- started in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the hydroelectric power station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what happened to your job when the war started against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime before April they arrived, the JNA units arrived of the former JNA, and took control of the Mostar dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did that mean that you lost your job at the -- at the power station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, I registered as -- I was -- I joined the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up. We're having difficulty hearing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you move a bit closer to the microphone and try to speak up a little bit. You don't have to -- this is okay, but also try to speak up a little bit. Now, you told the Court that you were joining the civilian protection in Mostar. During that period, what was the relationship between the -- between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims in the protection -- in the protection force? How would you describe that relationship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning the relationship was good. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did that change over time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did change over time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what was the reason? Why did it change? Can you give -- can you elaborate a bit on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was a change when they in actual fact took control in the town of Mostar, and all the main institutions came under the control of the HDZ and military structures, that they should be under the command of the HVO and the HDZ, which was their power.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just -- just to be sure because you say that they took control of the town of Mostar, who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I mean the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then you also said that they took control of the main institutions and that they came under the control of the HDZ. Can you give us some examples of what kind of institutions came -- got under the control of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time there still existed joint HDZ and SDA structures, politically speaking. However, in May or June already you couldn't even leave Mostar without the approval, without a certificate being issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you say May or June, can you also give the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I'm going to repeat my question. You've been referring they took over institutions. Could you give specific examples of institutions that were taking over, that were being taken over by the HDZ? And could you also explain how they would take over an institution like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make an observation. We're running out of time, constantly being told we have to move faster and faster. Much of this information has been given by other witnesses. If we -- if we run out of time today, it will not be because of the Defence, it's because we're going over old material.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is really -- this is something I think it's important for the witness to tell this, and I will move as swiftly as possible, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's also necessary to let him answer. You just asked a question and he still hasn't answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, Witness, could you please answer the questions that I just put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, mostly large buildings such as the mechanical engineering school of the university which they took over and turned it into their own military police headquarters. And then all the other buildings that used to house institutions of the town of Mostar on the right bank, they would take them over, place their military police and nobody would be allowed entry any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time in July 1992, when you changed your position, that you no longer -- that you joined another unit, and which unit was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I then transferred to SIS. The minister in charge was Raljak Vesic [as interpreted]. And that man Zoric who was still in the army, they asked him to establish a special police force, and since I was a mountaineer, I kind of fit the profile and I transferred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions for clarification. You said you were transferred to the SIS. Now, what does the SIS stand for, and was this the ABiH SIS or the HVO SIS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the SIS of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what does SIS stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the main police. It was called SIS then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you mentioned the person who was in charge of -- of SIS, and I think we didn't catch the name really well in the transcript. Could you repeat the name of the person who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, again during this period, and we're now in the period July -- let me first ask you. Up until what period of time did you serve for the SIS? Can you give a date when you actually stopped working for the SIS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been the 15th or the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And during this -- this period up, you know, from July 1992 until April 1992, can I again ask you how -- what was the role of the HVO in Mostar during this period? Did -- did the tensions increase or did they remain the same between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, maybe you should ask him about SIS again. I'm going to ask the question. We know that we -- you worked in SIS from July 1992 to April 1993. What did you do there? Were you a secretary, a guard? What were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked on the security of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was exactly your job, to guard the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] Guard duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Continue, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think that last answer wasn't really catched by the interpreters, so if we could repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's me ask you this then also. How many people were working in the building of the SIS that you guarded? Could you give us the number of people that were working for the SIS at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were about 10 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, coming back again to my question that I posed a bit earlier, what can you say about the relationship between the Croats and Muslims in Mostar during this period July 1992, April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship was always a bit strained. They didn't want us to have an army of our own. They wanted the HVO to be the only military force in the territory of Mostar. They wanted them to have all the control and to dispose of personnel and decide on further actions in the fight against the enemy. And they always wanted to put us under their command. They didn't want us to have our own command, and they practically cut us off from Sarajevo, the capital of BH, and we didn't even have passage towards Jablanica because a bridge was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just for the record, you keep referring to "they". Who are you referring to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did there come a time in September 1992 that something happened to the Sarajevo bank, and can you explain what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH dinar was introduced for the first time, and it was deposited in the Sarajevo bank. After that, HVO units, I don't know exactly which, arsoned that bank with all the money in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you witness this yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we have a basis for this? I mean, if the gentleman is going to lead the witness and he is going to be introducing this new evidence which we have heard now for the very first time, at least he should lay a proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, how did you learn about the fact that this bank was being set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That bank was located near a department store. It was a large building, and everybody saw the smoke when it was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how do you know that it was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because HV units blocked the road and did not let anyone pass or come near.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake, because in line 20 there is HV. In the interpretation it was HVO. Maybe we should inquire and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, you've said that HV units blocked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, get clarification whether it was Croatian army that the unit belonged to or HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I think you've heard the question of the Judge. Which units were actually blocking the streets? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, there's a bundle of exhibits that are on your desk, and I would like you to look at Exhibit number 619.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a daily report dated the 21st October 1992, and it's signed by -- by Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did you get a chance to read this document yesterday when we met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, let me read out a paragraph, the second paragraph of this document. It says the following: "Under orders from the defence department and on the basis of decisions from the HVO Presidency, we captured the following features in the town during the day: The post office, the building of the MUP, and the police station. We also interrupted the work of Radio Mostar BH. We also blocked all the roads and took all the check-points in the town." Can you -- can you read this -- do you read this paragraph which I just read out? And could I ask you, was this indeed -- did this indeed happen in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If you could then move to another exhibit which is Exhibit 01654.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a little question in between? Witness, do you know who the Defence Minister was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't quite hear the number you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And this, Your Honours, is again a report from Valentin Coric dated the 12th of March, 1993, and it's a report on the work of the military police and the control of the security situation in Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, again, did you get an opportunity to read this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: As I just said, we're now in March 1993, and here again it talks -- it gives details about the control of the military police in Mostar, and I'll just read you out one paragraph which is near the end of the -- of the report where it says: "All entrances to the town are covered by check-points of nine permanent military police officers 24 hours a day. The town itself is controlled by four permanent military police patrols constantly at readiness for two military police platoons, one on the left bank and one on the right, of 32 military police officers each." Now, again is it correct? Does this give a good description or a correct description of the control of the military police in Mostar in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric. You will have the right to cross-examine. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I will be very brief. This translation is not consistent with the original. That's all I wanted to say. Those who seriously work on this will be able to ascertain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... continue with my examination without interruptions like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's all very well for Mr. Bos to say that. It was a perfectly serious and responsible interruption and one that the Trial Chamber should take seriously. And, Your Honour, while I'm on my feet, a couple of other things quite quickly. This witness obviously has no personal knowledge whatsoever of the facts contained in these documents. He's not competent to testify about them. And, Your Honour, if the testimony that he's given about the arson of the -- of the bank is the only testimony to be given on that, it's irresponsible for the Prosecution to make a suggestion of arson based on this kind of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this document seems to establish that the military police was controlling the town. You who were at the time there, did you have that impression, that the military police was controlling passages, buildings, access roads? I see that there are several patrol -- patrols constantly on duty. Was that the impression that you had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And there was a curfew imposed just before the attack on the border from 4.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m. And they used combat vehicles to move around town and closed down catering establishments, coffee bars, restaurants, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have been told that there is a translation problem. In one passage we see that part of the town was controlled by military police it says. I think it was civilian police. Was there also a civilian police force in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were they a small force or a large force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how many men they had, but they existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we now move to March, April 1993. Did there come a time when tensions -- did around this time tensions increase even further between the Muslims and the Croats in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me show you one more document, and this is document 1868 in the bundle. And I'll just ask you a quick question about this. This is an HVO document dated the 14th of April, 1993. The heading doesn't say 1993, but if you read the text, you will see that there's reference to the year 1993. And, Witness, does this document which you read yesterday confirm that -- that the HVO reacted to these increased tensions by planning more intense fight control over the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question, Your Honour. It's so leading. I don't know what was told to the witness yesterday during the proofing session. We certainly didn't get any proofing notes. It is so suggestive. Why not just ask the gentleman what he knows and we can get his testimony. That is the best evidence, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Mr. Karnavas. You're right. Mr. Bos, you are really leading, because you're asking him on the basis of that document if the document is consistent with the situation that you are describing for him. That's not what you should be doing in your question. If you want to achieve that result, you should tell him, "We see this document. You just said that the police had intensified their work. There was increased control, curfew, et cetera. Can you also confirm that the police really had control?" He will say yes, and then "What else do you have to say?" you would say. And he would say, "In my eyes, it was an increase in tensions or I don't know what." So, Mr. Bos, please try to reformulate and proceed differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even in the civil law system the Judges would not allow themselves to ask this kind of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe to the Court the situation in April 1993 in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were clashes and skirmishes between the army and the HVO, and there was conflict in -- among top military authorities. They wanted to preserve their control, their military police, arrested members of the army and took them to the mechanical engineering school where they would keep them for two or three days. They would release some of them immediately. They would keep others for a longer time. They mistreated some of them, and thus the tensions were rising.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really apologise for this intervention, but I think it would be important to draw your attention to the first sentence in this document, because we see from it that the document was adopted because of the balance of powers and the situation in Konjic. It would be therefore relevant to find out what the witness knows about Konjic. The question of Mostar is not really relevant to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, it surely is relevant for document because it says "Plan for intensified control over the town of Mostar." But I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did you know what was going on in Konjic at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Witness, as -- as the way you've described the situation in April 1993, looking again at this exhibit 1868, would that confirm the situation as you just described?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're coming back to the same thing, Mr. Bos. You are again proceeding in the same way that was objected to before, and maybe it is not with this witness at all that you should be discussing these matters. If the witness told you that the situation deteriorated, then you can ask him other things then about this document. If he doesn't know the document, it's difficult to use it as a basis for obtaining any answers from the witness. You can achieve the same result by asking him different questions. For instance: Witness, you told us that you were on a security detail. Were you guarding the building of the SIS every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of those months, specifically April, did you feel at your level an intensification of security efforts? Did they ask you to double the shifts? Did you have increased workload? Did you observe at your level a change of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, the SIS building that I was guarding was not subject to any increased security. However, security was intensified outside in the street. They brought in a large number of soldiers in camouflage uniforms from outside. I think they were military police. The curfews started at 4.00 p.m. You could not move around town. They would be walking all over the town. Stjepan Radica Street that was close to the Vranica building in Mostar, and that's where army people had their favourite coffee-shops. They would come in their combat vehicles, dressed in camouflage uniforms, and close the cafes down. And they were -- they were imposing a feeling of uncertainty among the citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You who worked in the SIS and in the HVO, you certainly talked to other people, your work colleagues. What you just described, those increased patrols and security, what was the reason for it, if there was a reason? Maybe we'll establish that there was no particular reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With such a large number of check-points and the other things, I don't think it was really without any reason. I think it was all part of a plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, if one looks at the date of this document, 14th of April, did something important happen to you on the next day, the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 15th of April, I was already -- well, on the 15th or 16th, I'd already left town and joined the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was that an individual decision of your own initiative, or were any actions taken against you and maybe other Muslim policemen in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was at my own initiative, because I saw that there might be a conflict, and nobody could tell me over there what to do. So I joined my original unit where I had been before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Bos, for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, we've just heard a detail here. He said, "I joined my original unit." So what was your original unit, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that you were placed at the disposal of the HVO SIS by the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's not how it was. When Mr. Zoric crossed to set up the SIS and the special police, before that, I discussed this with him and I wanted to be in the special MUP units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In the record we read the name of Zoric. That could not be Coric; right? It's correct that it is Zoric, not Coric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoric, Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges who Mr. Zoric was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was -- well, he worked in the police in 1992 before the conflict, as far as I know. He worked in the Kameni MUP, as we used to call it, where the state security was. I don't know what he actually did before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did eventually in April -- Witness, could you please. Eventually in April, did it eventually ended up in an armed clash between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April the clash was on the 19th of April. It was called in Mostar the sniper war, although there was shooting afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were you involved in this sniping war? Can you explain in what way you were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, we were located at the Mostar hotel. Mostar hotel was the last stronghold of the BH army, if I can put it that way, before Santiceva, Cernica and Donja Mahala, those streets and areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what happened on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the 19th of April, they wanted to throw us out of Mostar hotel, and we started to defend ourselves and they attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who do you refer to when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how long did this attack last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the -- there were general tensions for about 10 days before we had to leave Hotel Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know more specifically which units were involved in this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say specifically what the units were, although it was the HVO army. Now, which units, I really can't say. And over there by Pepi -- or what shall I call it, near the hospital where there was Juka Prazina who, with sower, as we call it, kept this street under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said that it lasted about 10 days. How did it end? Why did it end after 10 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was up at the front line when suddenly UNPROFOR turned up with three or four APCs, and the late Arif Pasalic arrived as well, and quite simply, he demanded that we withdraw. He said that this had been agreed by the politicians, that it was an agreement between the HDZ and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that there was some sort of cease-fire agreed after 10 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'll ask you to look at two more documents. One is document 2146.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document dated the 30th of April 1993. It's signed by Ramo Maslesa, and it's addressed to the MUP of the BiH, to the minister of the MUP BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who Ramo Maslesa was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramo Maslesa was at the time the main person in the police. He was in the CRD. He was the chief there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This document talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, could you explain what CRD stands for, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The public security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, this document talks about joint patrols in Mostar. Is it correct that there were joint patrols after that cease-fire was agreed in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before all this firing, it was agreed that none of the armies, neither the HVO or the BH army -- or, rather, that they should all withdraw and go back to barracks, and that just the military police, the joint military police, should patrol town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did -- did this happen? You say they should patrol town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it never happened in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they couldn't reach an agreement about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that this document talks about the fact that -- that it was difficult in getting an agreement on these joint patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I then ask you to look at document 2169. And this is a document dated the 1st of May, the next day, 1993, and it's signed by commander Midhat Hujdur. Witness, do you know who Midhat Hujdur is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Mostar Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did -- was he in fact your direct commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, did you get a chance to read through this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Does this document accurately reflect the situation on the ground at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we're now moving to -- we're now moving to the 9th of May. You can close the document. Can you tell the Court where you were on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, as a military policeman, I was providing security to the command, and I was stationed in the Kluz department store, which is where the logistics was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where is the Kluz department store located in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Stjepan Radic Street. And as the building -- the Vranica building is linked to this building. They make up a compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, in the morning hours, at 4.30 a.m. or 5.00, there was heavy shelling suddenly on the Vranica building -- at the Vranica building and the Kluz building that I was in. They were heavily shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you describe what -- what you did when the building was being shelled at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the entrance shells fell. Part of the wall was blown away. We weren't able to leave. We were down in the basement. The logistics building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said at 4.30 or 5.00 a.m. On what basis do you say that was the time this happened? Did you have a detail which allowed you to specify? Did you hear artillery noise and you looked at your watch, or were you standing guard? Can you tell us how you know that that was the exact time, between 4.30 and 5.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it had -- day had just broken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 4.30 and 5.00 most of the people were asleep. Were you asleep or were you awake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were all asleep except for the guard that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what woke you up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was woken up by the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: With how many people were you in the Kluz building, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Kluz building there were six or seven people together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Witness, did there come a time that morning that you -- that you heard something over the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That morning, I don't know at what time, on Radio Herceg-Bosna it was reported that the HVO had taken control -- or, rather, launched a broad action to cleanse the town and that this was related to Santic sector, Crnica, and Donja Mahala, that area. Afterwards, they announced that all members of the BH army on the right bank who were in their houses would be given white sheets -- should put white sheets over the balcony to hand in their weapons and they wouldn't be harmed and that all the wounded and anybody who needed help in hospital would be able to get that help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've just said that on the radio they said that the cleansing operation had started. Now, we must be quite precise here. Was it a speaker, a presenter, a radio announcer, or somebody else who was talking over the radio? Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a presenter and her name was Zlata Brbor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was it that she said exactly, to the best of your recollections? So it was a woman, Zlata.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did she say to the best of your recollections and be as precise as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, she said that the HVO had taken -- had engaged in broad action to cleanse the town. And this replied -- applied to Santiceva, Crnica, and Donja Mahala, and that they were asked to surrender, all the Muslims who had rifles in their homes should put out a white sheet and that nothing would happen to them if they did that and if they handed in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So somebody who hears this word "cleansing" might not understand. What did that mean? What did this mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they just wanted to expel us and force us to go to the left bank of the river Neretva to take control of the right bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that's what the presenter said, did she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the presenter. You asked me what cleansing meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that the lady presenter said over the radio at the beginning, and this is on lines 12 and 13, that the HVO had launched a widespread operation to cleanse the town. So my question to you is this: Was it this lady presenter who said that they were going to cleanse the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The presenter said that the HVO had taken on a broad operation to liberate Mostar and that referred to Santiceva, Crnica, and Donja Mahala in particular. And then I told the guys -- when you asked about cleansing, I said that they wanted to expel us to the left bank, liberating the right bank. So that's it. And I know what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's be clear. So the lady presenter said that the HVO was going to liberate, and you translated the word "liberate" as meaning cleansing. All right. So with my questions, I have cleared the matter up. A question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness CV, an explanation, please. You said you were woken up by the shelling. Now, the Kluz department store where you were standing guard, was that shelled as well? That's my first question. Was there fighting going on at that particular location? That's my second question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was shelled and, yes, there was fighting. Well, I don't know what you mean by "fighting" exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that it was announced over the radio that they were going to liberate or cleanse the town. Now, my question is: In the spot you were, the store was shelled, I understand, and were there soldiers that were fighting in or around the building, the department store?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what forces were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the Vranica building and around the Kluz department store, there were a number of HVO units. There was the military police. There was the 3rd Battalion and their anti-terrorist platoon or something like that. And there was the Knez Domagoj Brigade from Capljina. And there was -- well, some others, too. Something with respect to the army. They had this machine-gun known as the sower controlling the area, and that's where they were doing the shooting from. And they also shelled us using heavy weapons, because at Bijeli Brijeg there was a tank, and there was a PAT too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a clarification for the -- for the record. On line 12 it says -- when you talk about the units that -- when you identify the unit, it says there was the third month, and I think that's probably not correct. Can you tell me again which unit was the 3rd? Can you tell that again for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you actually try to defend the Kluz building that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the Kluz building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were in the Kluz building up until about 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Kluz building you could go in through the basement, the other side, and enter the building that was above it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to go back to an important question. We've heard a number of witnesses on this, and the question was raised, so I'm going to ask you this question. At the time, you were a military -- part of the military personnel stationed in this Kluz building. And you said that on the 9th of May you were sleeping when you suddenly heard artillery firing. As a military man, as a soldier, before the 9th of May, did your command tell you at any point in time that the ABiH was going to attack the HVO? Were there any orders to that effect, any preparations or anything said about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never? Never? You affirm that this was never said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were never told, you soldiers, your unit or group, that an attack was being prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether this is important or not, but page 36, line 6, the answer that they were in the Kluz building up until about 10.00, I thought I heard the witness say in the French translation une dizaine d'heures, which would actually have a different sense of 10 hours, being there for 10 hours rather than until 10.00. I wonder if that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you tell us when you left the Kluz building? Could you tell us that again? Around what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left the Kluz building at about 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown this drawing that the witness drew up yesterday in proofing. And this hopefully will help explain a little bit what the witness did on the 9th and 10th of May. Have that on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you -- that you made this drawing yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you just explain the Court a little bit the various locations that you have drawn up here so that the Judges will know which building is which? Maybe let me just ask you. Where is the Kluz building on this drawing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Kluz building is exactly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the building on the left, is that -- what's the building on the left? Maybe you can just explain all the various buildings on this drawing. Just tell the Judges which buildings they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance to Kluz, and the building is joined to this one over here, the Vranica building. Between those two buildings there's a passage. And there are columns, and above the columns are flats. What I've drawn here is the entrance to this building here. So you could enter the building underneath Kluz, through the basement corridor and come up the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you say that the building was connected with the Vranica building which I presume is the building on the left. How was it connected? How were you able to go from one building to the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this building here you could go to this building. There was a terrace linking the two buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So -- and where was this terrace situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up at the top of the building. That's how they were linked. You could go via the terrace over into the next building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you left the Kluz building at 10.00 a.m., where were you planning to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through this passageway. You could run across. And there was another entrance there on this side where the courtyard was. You could enter the building that way. But it was a wide space to run across, and one of our men tried and he was wounded in the leg. So we gave up running across.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why did you want to go to the other building? Why did you want to go to the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we wanted to link up with our unit. In this first building we were no longer able to hold the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And which other units were in the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I -- when we refer to the Vranica building, it is linked -- Vranica was where the 4th Corps was, and here, to begin with, was this brigade, the 41st Motorised Brigade, and they were linked with a cellar, a basement. So you could enter one side, go through the basement and come up the other side. This whole building was linked via the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how many members of the 41st Brigade were in the Vranica building on the 9th and 10th of May, and how many of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the brigade command there might have been no more than 20 to 30 of us, if that. In the Vranica corps -- in the corps in the Vranica building, the corps there, maybe 10 to 15 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. It's 9.30 [sic]. Should we have a break now, or should I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Time flies by. Mr. Registrar, how much time has the Prosecution used? Let's take a 20-minute break, and we'll reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we left off with the drawing, and we left off around 10.00 a.m. that you were leaving the Kluz building. Now, could you tell the Court where did you go when you left the Kluz building? And if you wish, you can show on the drawing where you went.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already said, since it was possible to reach this entrance from the basement, we wanted to physically join our brigade. Since that was impossible because we had one wounded, we returned to the building, and then we went upstairs, taking the stairs, and the only possibility for us was to reach the building of the brigade across rooftops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you ended up on the roof of the Vranica building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got to the roof of the Vranica building and crossed over to the brigade building, we were unable to get in because there was the elevator entrance with bars on the doors that we couldn't get through. Since there was firing at the brigade building from PATs and PAMs, anti-aircraft guns and anti-aircraft machine-guns, one shell hit the elevator and created a passage. Since there was a number of us and we couldn't get in safely then, we waited for the night, for the cover of the night to get into the building of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that during that whole day you were on the roof of the Vranica building before you actually entered the building during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And with how many people were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six to seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can you indicate on the map from which side the HVO was targeting the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this side over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What did you eventually do when you were able during the night to get into the Vranica building? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got into the building, then we took the stairs to get down to the command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And was this the command of the brigade or the command of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you were there -- when you got there, is it correct that you encountered your father there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I got there to the brigade command and even before while I was still climbing down the stairs, I was told that I shouldn't worry but my father was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did he get wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I lived close to the Vranica building, he had left his home to go to the brigade, and when he was just entering the building he was hit by a small calibre bullet in his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was your father wearing a uniform? Was he a member of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now -- so you entered the brigade command on the night of 9th of May. Did you stay there overnight in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent the whole night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did you do on the morning of the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the morning of the 10th day [as interpreted], after a whole night on guard duty, we were resting, and I heard when somebody was passing by and saying that if my father isn't transferred to the hospital immediately he would bleed to death. When I heard that, I went to our communications centre because the communication with the army was cut off at the time. We could only communicate with the HVO. I managed to reach one of those people there and asked them to put me -- to put Vlado Topic on the telephone because we were family friends. And if I remember well, he had said on radio Herceg-Bosna that nobody would be deprived of medical assistance, that everybody would be given access to the hospital. So when I got Topic on the line, I told him that my father had been wounded, that he was bleeding out, that he needed to be moved urgently and hospitalised. And since we were family friends, he asked me why we were not surrendering, and I replied, "We have no one to surrender to. We were just defending ourselves. We were not attacking anyone." And I told him not to come with large vehicles that they normally used to move around town. I told him to bring a small car instead, bringing no more than 2 men. He said he would do so and then the line was cut off. I managed to reach him again to get a telephone connection 15 minutes later, and I got Vasic on the phone, and I had a clash with him. If you look at my statement, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. Just one clarification. You've said that you contacted the person named Vlado Topic. What was the position of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what position he held exactly at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Why did you call him? Why did you think that he could help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were family friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me then ask you. You were talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a second. Franjo Topic, in fact. Franjo Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe you could spell the name for us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: F-r-a-n-j-o, Franjo Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted you and you said that about 15 minutes later a second person called. What was the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Lasic, who was then commander for the south zone, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miro Lasic, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did Lasic tell you when you got him on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got him on the phone, he asked me whether the wounded person was wounded or bleeding, and then he said we had killed his brother, and then we started shouting at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why did you shout at him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I realised he was not going to help me. And on top of that, he started to threaten me. And then I threatened him, and then we both hung up on each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you then describe what happened during -- on the 10th of May, during that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the 10th of May, since we had no where to go and the civilians from that building were together with us in the basement, and we had to move into the entranceway from time to time so that they couldn't get near us, and it could have been 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning when, although we didn't know it yet, but we found out when we got out. Juka Prazina's unit was firing at us using incendiary bullets from the school building, shooting at random at the first, then the second, then the fifth floor, and some of the shells were falling into the basement. And one of those cluster rounds injured the daughter of Batlak as well as one of the young men who worked in communications. Since everybody was panic-stricken, the residents of that building practically pushed us out into the entranceway. When we got there, we realised there was no way we could fight back. And there were civilians there. Those people were demanding over the bullhorn that we surrender, and one of the civilians negotiated with them, and they said that all the civilians should get out and they would be safe. No harm would come to them. Since HVO soldiers were stoned or something, we didn't want to surrender in our uniforms. We decided it was better to change into civilian clothes and surrender and get out with the civilians. When we changed into civilian clothes, we left the building, together with the residents, and we walked out with hands behind our back -- behind our head, and we walked through to the economic school. They let all the Croats go immediately, and they told the Muslims to walk to the Velez stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Just one clarification. On page 44, line 6, you say that the HVO were stoned or something. What do you mean by that, and why -- why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the way they acted you could see that their behaviour was altered. They kept threatening to kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just focus your attention again on the map, because you testified that you were taken to the economic school. Can you indicate on the map where this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've said that when the group arrived at the -- at the economic school that a selection was made. First of all, who -- who did this? Who made this selection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of Juka Prazina's unit, and there were other HVO soldiers who all had the insignia, those patches with the flag, or armbands on the left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You stated they all released the Croats immediately and told the Muslims to walk to the Velez stadium. Should I conclude from this that you went to the Velez stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Elderly Muslims who were 70 years old and over were told that they were going to be taken to the stadium, and we, the others, were left to stay at the economic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How many -- so you stayed at the economic school. How many other people stayed there from your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since there were also civilians there, and perhaps 30, maybe more, of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Where were you taken, you and these other 30 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were then taken to -- we didn't know where exactly we were being taken. We were going through the avenue, and we finally reached the tobacco factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown on e-court Exhibit 09613.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: 09613. Witness, I'm waiting for the photograph to appear on the screen. Can you also see the photograph now in front of you on the television? Witness, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the building of the tobacco.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can you indicate on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And maybe the witness can use the electronic marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you indicate where you and the other 30 people who were with you were put when you arrived at this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not really sure that's the right picture, but here on the right side when you are entering the buildings, on the right-hand side you go straight ahead and then there is a small semicircle near the road, and then it goes straight ahead. I'm not sure this picture really shows that, because at the time there were no cars outside. Maybe we were somewhere here. As this road goes, perhaps we were at this point, but I cannot really recognise it from this picture. I think we were further to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are commenting on the photograph that we see on our screens or on something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He actually did make a couple of drawings on the e-court photograph. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, Witness, when you arrived there, who was at the tobacco institute? Were there people there when you arrived? Maybe move a little bit away from the microphone because you're a bit too close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were coming, the first thing I saw was that there were a lot of people there, including Branko Kvesic. He approached me, took me by the shoulders, and we had an exchange. And outside this building there were many, many people, some troops, and some civilians. I think all the top men of the HDZ and the HVO were there. Apart from Branko Kvesic, I saw Petar Zelenika. Misic later came there too. He was commander of the 4th battalion. There was Juka Prazina with his unit. There were many people. I couldn't take it all in. But right before us there was a crowd, including civilians, outside the tobacco institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Just one follow-up question on what you just testified. You've mentioned a couple of names, Branko Kvesic, Petar Zelenika, and then you referred to a person named Misic. Do you know the first name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Misic was a man whom everybody called Old Misic. He was commander of the 4th Battalion. He approached us. He asked 10 men to be singled out, to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then he said, "I'll execute them all."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's -- let's go step-by-step. So when you arrived with your group on the -- at the tobacco station, just explain from there what happened to you in as detailed as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we arrived we were lined up. Before that I had that exchange with Branko Kvesic. He asked me why I hadn't come to see him. I said I didn't want to shoot at my own people. Tuta was there as well. And then Kvesic told Tuta, "This man used to be in our ranks. Then he crossed over and started shooting at us." Then Tuta approached me, took out his Motorola and starting hitting me, cursing my balija mother. I told him my mother was not a balija, she was a Catholic woman. And after that he started hitting me even harder. Then a man called Dujma approached. He was with another man, Slezak, blonde and thin, and they started hitting me with the rifle butt, and that went on for some time. They hit me more than once. Then Juka offered his hand to help me up. He said that nobody was to hit me any more. And then, as I was still crouching, he hit me -- he kicked me in the head and I fell to the ground again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you referred to Juka, which Juka is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Juka Prazina, who was -- who had crossed over to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, were other -- were any other members of your group also being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just Pobric, Pobric. They beat Pobric too. Tuta hit him with the handle of a pistol over the head, and he started bleeding straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sometime earlier you spoke about Misic doing things. When did that actually happen, and can you explain again what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he entered the institute, as he walked towards us, he said he should be given 10 men to execute, and then he said, "Not 10, all of them." Then Juka said, "Those you take into custody you can execute. The others will go for the exchange and be exchanged for my soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, while you were there at the tobacco institute, did you at any time see a television crew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my right there was a camera, and I saw that it said HTV2 on the camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now like to show Exhibit 08987, and -- which is a video of a couple of minutes, and it will be presented through Sanction. So we will be able to play that video from our desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we show it in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We will need to go into private session. I don't know if there is any public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the tobacco factory, we were put into a bus and taken to the civilian police, the building of the civilian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where was this? Was this in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Visnjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you give the name of that village again? I think the interpreters didn't hear you quite well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Listica and is now Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And with how many people were you taken there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Listica, interpreter's correction. Listica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they took us from the tobacco factory to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how big was the group of people that actually went, was taken to Listica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 25 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where were you -- where were you put in the MUP station in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two small cells, and the ventilation was just a brick turned upside town with air coming through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you ever mistreated during this period that you were at the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you give me the names of the persons that -- that mistreated you, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think his name was Andabak, that he was Tuta's deputy. When we lined up in front of that MUP building, he set to straight away on Meho Zilic because he had worked in the DB beforehand, and he said that he was responsible for persecuting Croats. And then he was hit and then he was asked whether he was involved in the liberation of the left bank against the Serbs. I came forward. I was there. And I thought I would have an easier time. And he asked me whether I was at Hum. I said that that's not the left bank, and then he started beating me and kept saying that they fed us and that we stuck a knife in their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were any other people besides the person you referred to as Andabak who beated you or any of the other prisoners at the MUP station during the period that you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went down to those cells, at night two men came. Two uniformed men came during the night, Romeo and Takac. Romeo Blazevic and Ernest Takac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what did these two persons do that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Allegedly they had a piece of paper from the police giving them authorisation to interrogate the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did these two persons beat up prisoners that night, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Romeo, as soon as he entered the cell where I was, he immediately set to -- threw himself on me and said that I had thrown a bomb into a coffee bar. He had a truncheon in his hand and wanted to hit me on the head with it. I tried to defend myself, to protect myself, but at one point he took out a pistol and said that I should stick my thumbs into the pockets of my tracksuit, and whenever he tried to hit me, wanted to hit me, I still raised my hands to defend my body. I fell across a raised section of the cell. He took his rifle butt and hit me on the head and it started to bleed, and he left me like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, for how long were you kept detained at the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the station, MUP station, I think we were there for about seven or eight days. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you -- do you recall during this period that you were ever asked to sign a paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before they transported us to the other prison, the other camp, they asked us to sign a piece of paper saying that nobody had touched us over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you and the other prisoners sign that paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We all signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When were you -- where were you taken next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to add a question on this period. You have described an incident where you were ill-treated. Was that the only incident or have beatings being repeated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't the only incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you be a bit more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After -- well, we were made to do forced labour at the pool. They said it was Tuta's pool, their pool, the city pool. We worked there. And as it was an open space, at a given moment a driver turned up. He was the driver to the minister for social welfare or whatever it's called. I was sitting down by the pool, and without asking anything, he just kicked me in the ribs. And I fell down and hit me head on the concrete. And he pulled out a pistol, wanted to kill me as I grabbed his legs, and one of the guards prevented him from doing that. They took me back down there. And on another occasion, a tall guy wearing a uniform came into our cell, and later on he told me that it was Cikota's brother. Or somebody told me it was Cikota's brother. And together with him there were seven or eight men, and they beat me. And at one point Andabak or whatever his name was, this deputy, put a pistol to my head and said he would kill me, and he pulled the trigger and put the pistol back. And then afterwards, Cikota told me to put my tongue out, stick my tongue out, and he put out a cigarette butt on my tongue and then he made me eat that. Afterwards, he forced me to hit my head against the wall 10 times as strongly as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did that answer your question, Judge? Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, so where were you transferred after you left the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They transferred us to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: With how many people were you transferred to Ljubuski? Was this the complete group that was in the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That complete group was transferred to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you describe where you were taken when you arrived at Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to Ljubuski, and at the time there was the military police there, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you say the military police was there, are you saying that the guards of Ljubuski were military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a prison belonging to the military police, and they stood guard over us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So please continue. Where were you taken when you got at Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- when we went inside, into the Ljubuski building, in the hallway they told us that all -- we should leave all our belongings, everything we had brought with us, and then they took us to a cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how big was this cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As there were about 25 to 30 of us, the cell was so small that we couldn't all sit down in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Ljubuski for perhaps 15, 10 days. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But my question was during this 10, 15 days, did you always stay in that particular cell with the whole group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The next day they came from Siroki Brijeg and took eight or ten men to continue working on the swimming pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were you included in this group or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I stayed at Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you ever have to perform forced labour while being detained in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken only once to forced labour at Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the front line facing the Serbs. We dug trenches for them there. I was given a sledgehammer, and we had to climb up rocks and make steps for them so they wouldn't slip. They said the next shift would include men who had been in Mostar. And there were many men killed in their unit, because when they were getting down this reservoir with petrol, with a fuel, they couldn't get it up and it ended up killing a lot of them. I thought I was again going to be beaten because this wood --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said something using some words that the interpreter doesn't understand. Could he repeat the last thing he said about the wooden handle?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreters didn't get the last part of what you just said. You said something about wood. Could you repeat that sentence because the interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That wooden sledgehammer. At the end of the handle was cracked. It was not smooth. And to avoid being called out to work again, I let this wood slide across my hands so as to injure my hands and to be unable to do forced labour again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever ill-treated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. The witness has said that many were killed. I am quoting from page 62, line 6, 7. "Because when they were getting down this reservoir with petrol, a fuel, they didn't get it up and it ended up killing a lot of them." I, frankly, do not understand this, and I would be grateful if -- if you could explain, Witness. Maybe it was difficult to translate or whatever. What reservoir were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what date it was, but HVO units filled a tank with petrol and with bombs and ammunition, and they wanted, once reaching Hit, to let this tank drop and explode at the bridge which was the only crossing against -- across Neretva and thus cut off the entire Donja Mahala. And they were looking for a man to be the driver of that tank. They looked for a person from the camp to be -- to drive that tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And how did people get killed in this context? You said many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
